evidence: Measured in 6 of 6 MONDAYS hemp SKUs at 0.09–0.3% of total volatiles (0.018–0.06mg per chew).

consumer_summary.what_it_is: Caryophyllene oxide is a naturally occurring epoxide, a type of oxygen-containing molecule formed when plants metabolize other terpenes. It is a key contributor to the earthy, woody, and slightly spicy aromas found in many culinary herbs and aromatic plants. You likely encounter it whenever you smell fresh oregano, steep a cup of holy basil tea, or enjoy the complex bitterness of a hoppy beer.
consumer_summary.found_in: This compound is widely distributed in nature, appearing in over 400 recorded species. It is notably found in hops (Humulus lupulus), oregano (Origanum vulgare), holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum), and lavender (Lavandula latifolia).
consumer_summary.why_researchers_care: Researchers are drawn to caryophyllene oxide for its broad biological activity, particularly its potential to interact with cellular pathways involved in inflammation, microbial defense, and cell survival. Much of the excitement stems from its role in the "entourage effect" of cannabis and its ability to trigger specific cellular processes like ferritinophagy in tumor cell lines. The strongest evidence so far comes from individual cohort and human observational studies (Oxford level 2b), which are guiding scientists toward targeted clinical applications.

structure_function.statement: May support the body's natural defenses against certain microbes.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Researchers are exploring whether caryophyllene oxide can influence tumor cell survival, particularly through pathways like ferritinophagy (the degradation of the iron-storage protein ferritin). If this bears out, it could become a valuable natural compound in the development of targeted antineoplastic therapies.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled human clinical trial measuring tumor marker progression and cellular iron regulation in patients over a 6-to-12 month period.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Scientists are investigating whether this molecule can effectively neutralize harmful bacteria and fungi. If confirmed, it could offer a new plant-derived tool for combating resistant microbial strains.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A larger, randomized, double-blind clinical trial applying a topical caryophyllene oxide formulation to localized skin infections, measuring microbial clearance rates over 14 days.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Early animal work points toward potential analgesic properties, prompting researchers to ask if it can safely modulate pain pathways in humans. If successful, it might provide a non-habit-forming alternative for managing discomfort.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A Phase I/II first-in-human trial administering standardized oral doses of caryophyllene oxide to healthy volunteers subjected to acute pain stimuli, assessing pain scores and safety over a 24-hour period.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Observational data hints at a sedative effect, leading researchers to explore whether it can improve sleep architecture. If this holds up, it could be utilized in natural sleep aids to help people fall asleep faster and stay asleep longer.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial in adults with mild insomnia, using polysomnography to measure sleep latency and duration over a 4-week period.

associated_conditions.relationship: Studied as an intervention for in laboratory cell models.

consumer_summary.cautions: Laboratory studies indicate that highly concentrated doses can stimulate red blood cell breakdown (hemolysis), so intake should remain at normal dietary levels.
consumer_summary.evidence_at_a_glance: Best evidence so far includes human observational and individual cohort studies (Oxford level 2b), while much of the remaining literature consists of in vitro and animal research.
